22.0.0.en: 1 A slothful man is like a filthy stone; everyone hisses at his disgrace. 2 A slothful man is like the dung of a dunghill; everyone who picks it up shakes his hand.

22.0.1.en: The chapter begins with the two most dangerous enemies of wisdom, namely laziness and indulgence in pleasures. Parents long for their children to be better than themselves in manners, learning, knowledge and success in everything. Therefore he began by speaking of laziness, so that parents may not pamper their children, but that they may grow up serious in their lives. Then he speaks afterward about wisdom, that they may walk in a spirit of prudence in the Lord. He also affirms the discipline of a son if he sins. And he calls on children to flee from corrupt friendships and to cleave to wise friends.

22.0.2.en: For Ben Sira, slackness or laziness is the prominent mark of the fool. By his laziness the fool is a problem for himself and for others, for laziness has its effects on society. There is no one who wants to cleave to a lazy person.

22.0.3.en: Ben Sira speaks of the lazy young girl, whom no one wishes to marry, and who spends her life dependent on her parents [3-4]. And the impudent daughter, if she marries, brings shame upon her father and her husband [5].

22.0.4.en: The lazy man is like a defiled stone; everyone hisses at his shame [1].

22.0.5.en: Laziness drives a person to shame (Prov 24:30-34). He is like a stone soiled with filth; whoever looks at him is offended by him. It is said: "God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... male and female created he them" (Gen 1:16, 28). God is the Worker! Perhaps you wonder at this attribute, for rarely does a person fix his insight on God as the Worker. With boldness I say that it befits the image to be conformed to the original and to cleave to him, and to ask for his grace so as to bear the true image, one of whose marks is work!

22.0.6.en: After the Supreme Artist had brought into being this world, wonderful in its beauty, for the sake of man, and after He had created man as a king in his palace, "the garden of Eden", possessing authority, it is said: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." God was pleased with what He had made, not out of need of it, but because work pours happiness and joy upon man, whom He loves!

22.0.7.en: Thus He created us and placed us in the garden of Eden, and we had no need to work in order to eat and drink and take delight. But He wanted us to be like Him, so that we would work and keep the garden. Had our first parents not sinned, we would have worked without weariness, and would have found our joy in offering works of love to those around us, and all would rejoice in the common work of love.

22.0.8.en: It is said of God: "And he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it" (Gen 2:1-2). God's rest on the seventh day is not idleness, for He is always at work: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17). He completed the creation, and He continues to care for it and to be concerned for the salvation of man, whose nature he had corrupted.

22.0.9.en: As for us, our rest is not in fleeing from work. Though, for the rest of body and mind, we enjoy holidays, yet we work even in our sleep and our rest, through love. We work with wisdom and balance in every aspect of our spiritual, intellectual, psychological, scholarly, social and physical life, so that a person may enjoy creativity in what God has given him, to complete the work of his brothers in the other aspects.

22.0.10.en: The Apostle Paul took pride in that he supported himself and those with him through his work (Acts 20:34-36). And in his epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor 4:8-13) he made clear that he worked and toiled. In this he rebukes them, for in their slackness and laziness they thought of themselves as kings who do not do any work.

22.0.11.en: v Be occupied with what belongs to the Lord, or busy with your work, but do not be idle [1].

22.1.0.en: The Didascalia v In the beginning you could have worked without toil... because God Himself wanted this, but you did not allow it. For God did not mix work with toil. Had man experienced toil from the beginning, he would not have been afflicted with it afterward as a punishment. You can work and at the same time not reach the stage of hard labor, as in the case of the angels [2].

22.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom v Those who fully realize that all their work must aim at attaining the good life, and yet amuse themselves with temporal blessings; these I compare to people who seek a cure and medicine but do not know how to use it, and are not troubled over (their ignorance of its use). Therefore let us not excuse the sins we commit by pleading the circumstances of our surroundings or by attributing them to another person, but let us lay the blame on ourselves. For if our souls willingly give themselves up to laziness, they cannot escape defeat [3].

22.2.1.en: St. Anthony the Great The lazy man can be likened to the filth of dung; everyone who gathers it shakes his hand from it [2].

22.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom often attacked the lazy who are without work, and he made this clear in his homily In inscriptionem altaris [4]. And when he spoke of the poor he meant the toiling workers. He does not praise them for their poverty, but for their struggle in work, that they weary themselves in order to support their families.

22.4.0.en: v If you wish to uproot poverty, you will certainly uproot the whole structure of life, you will shatter your life. You will not find a sailor or a ship's pilot or a farmer or a builder, nor a weaver or a shoemaker or a carpenter or a smith or a tanner or a miller; you will find none of these workers nor any others... If all become rich, all will live in idleness, and everything will perish and be dissipated [5].

22.5.0.en: 3 An undisciplined son is a disgrace to his father, and a daughter only brings loss. 4 A prudent daughter is an inheritance to her husband, and a shameful daughter is a grief to her father. 5 The impudent one shames her father and her husband, and both of them treat her with contempt.

22.5.1.en: An undisciplined son is a shame to his father, and the birth of a foolish daughter is a loss to him [3].

22.5.2.en: An obstinate, undisciplined son shames his parents. As for the birth of an obstinate daughter, it is counted a loss in the family. A daughter lacking discipline is not tolerated by her husband and so she shames her parents; neither her husband nor her parents honor her.

22.6.0.en: A prudent daughter brings an inheritance to her husband, and a shameful daughter is a sorrow to her father [4].

22.7.0.en: An impudent daughter shames her father and her husband, and is despised by both of them [5].

22.8.0.en: 6 A tale out of season is like music in mourning, but stripes and instruction are wisdom at all times.

22.8.1.en: A word out of season is like music in a time of grief, but discipline and the teaching of wisdom are fitting at every time [6].

22.8.2.en: The Lord disciplines His children through love, and in the same spirit parents discipline their child (Heb 12:5-8). It seems that Ben Sira was groaning over the excessive pampering of children, especially in aristocratic circles, and he was also grieved over families that neglect the upbringing of their children. Note that the number of children whom families have spoiled has greatly increased. What occupied families was working with all their energies and praying that the Lord would give them children, without exerting any effort to bring them up as befits them as people of God.

22.8.3.en: The first one responsible for a child's upbringing is the family; and if the family fails, it befits the teachers to try to guide the children; and if the teachers fail, the police intervene to discipline the undisciplined.

22.8.4.en: Guiding children and disciplining them in a fitting manner is necessary, lest they grow up fools and lose a worthy life.

22.8.5.en: v The Lord disciplines human beings not out of hatred, for He suffered for our sake when He was able to destroy us because of our faults. He is the good Teacher who has full power to reprove with words of rebuke.

22.8.6.en: Words of rebuke are like a whip with which the idle mind of men is scourged. And while He scourges them, it is stirred to advise them. For those who are raised by words of praise are pricked by being blamed. And those whom blame cannot raise to salvation as though they were dead, rise to the truth through their accusation. "But stripes and instruction are fitting at all times for wisdom" [6].

22.9.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria He who teaches a fool is like one who mends a broken earthen vessel, and like one who tries to wake a man sunk in his sleep [7].

22.10.0.en: 7 He who teaches a fool mends a vessel of earthenware, 8 and rouses one sunk in his sleep. 9 He who speaks to a fool speaks to one who is drowsy; and when he has finished he says, "What?" 10 Weep for the dead, for he has lost the light, and weep for the fool, for he has lost his mind. 11 Weep less for the dead, for he is at rest, 12 but the life of the fool is worse than his death. 13 Mourning for the dead is seven days, but mourning for the fool and the hypocrite is all the days of his life. 14 Do not multiply words with the ignorant, and do not mingle with the dull. 15 Be on guard against him, lest he trouble you and defile you with his filth. 16 Turn away from him and you will find rest, and his folly will not grieve you. 17 What is heavier than lead? And what is he called but a fool? 18 Sand and salt and iron are lighter to bear than an ignorant man! 19 A framework of timber bound into a building is not loosened by an earthquake; so also the heart that relies on sound counsel is not afraid at all. 20 The heart that leans upon a wise opinion is like an ornament of sand on a polished wall. 21 As stakes set in a high place do not stand against the wind, 22 so the fearful heart of the fool, with its thoughts, does not stand against any terror. 23 The heart of the fool is afraid in its thoughts, but he who continues in the commandments of God at all times is never afraid.

22.10.1.en: Weeping over the fool is more bitter than weeping over a dead man. Therefore Ben Sira demands that children be kept apart from association with the fool, for the following reasons:

22.10.2.en: a. Because the life of the fool is worse than death.

22.10.3.en: b. He does not accept instruction, so speaking with him is a waste of time and causes weariness to the one who speaks with him.

22.10.4.en: c. Dealing with him is counted a burden on the soul, for he is heavier than lead and sand and salt and a block of iron.

22.10.5.en: d. The wise man takes a firm decision with which he defies the coming of an earthquake of troubles (Ps 112:7; Mt 7:24-27), but the fool is wavering, and the mere fear of troubles shatters him.

22.11.0.en: He who tells something to a fool is speaking to a sleeping man, and in the end he says: "What is this?" [8]

22.12.0.en: If children live faithfully and have what is necessary, they cover over the lowliness of their parents. [9]

22.13.0.en: But proud children, through scorn and lack of food, stain the nobility of their kin [10].

22.13.1.en: It does not befit the believer to despise children and infants, for the ill-behaved child does wrong to his family, and the child who walks in the way of truth is a blessing to it and supports it. For it was said of the repentance of the people of Nineveh:

22.13.2.en: v Oh, the harmony of repentance! What a wise and powerful sorrow! They did not leave even the animals outside the arrangement, but in marvelous ways obliged them also to cry out. They separated the calf from its mother, and deprived the lamb of its suckling.

22.13.3.en: They took the nursing infants from their mothers' arms. The mothers were put in one place and the infants in another, calling to one another and answering with mournful voices. The hungry infants seek the source of their milk, while the mothers, pricked by the instinct of motherhood, cry out toward their children in grieved voices.

22.13.4.en: The hungry infants cry out, seized by bitter cries for help, while the hearts of the mothers were tormented by the pains of natural affection. For this reason the inspired Word preserved their repentance as a universal model of how to live.

22.13.5.en: The elders grieved because of the chastisement with which they were threatened; they were in bitterness, in their old age.

22.13.6.en: The boys and the little ones lament with greater burning.

22.13.7.en: The poor sigh, while the rich forgot their comfort and put on the sackcloth that befits the sorrowful.

22.13.8.en: The king of Nineveh left his glory and his loftiness, turning toward disgrace. He left his crown, and put dust on his head, and took off the royal robe and wrapped himself in sackcloth. He left his high and glorious majesty, and crawled on the ground in lowliness. He left the luxury that belonged to him as a king, in order to grieve with the people. He became one of them when he saw the wrath of the Lord of all [7].

22.13.9.en: St. Basil the Great Weep for the dead, because he has left the light behind, and weep for the fool, because he has left the mind behind.

22.14.0.en: Weep with joy for the dead, because he is at rest, but the life of the fool is worse than death [11].

22.14.1.en: By saying: "Weep with joy for the dead, for he is at rest", he reveals that there is a blessed life after death, and not a cessation of life.

22.14.2.en: v True prudence is knowing what you do and what you do not do. He who possesses it does not cease from virtuous works, and will not be pierced by the deadly arrow of vice. So he who understands the words of prudence knows the difference between what is enticing and built upon deceit, and what calmly reminds us of the true way of practicing life... Give such prudence to him who builds his house, that he may lay the foundation upon a rock, that is, support it with faith in Christ, so that it is not shaken when the winds blow and the rains fall and the storms assail it (Mt 7:25) [8].

22.14.3.en: St. Basil the Great v Just as the body without the soul is dead, so the soul without the mind is idle (barren) and unable to inherit God [9].

22.14.4.en: v In the soul there is a mind that works, while in the body there is instinct. The mind makes the soul divine, and instinct corrupts the body (that is, if we satisfy our instincts and natural desires).

22.14.5.en: Instinct works in every body, but not every soul has the mind working in it. For this reason not every soul is saved [10].

22.15.0.en: St. Anthony the Great Mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but mourning for the fool lasts all the days of his life [12].

22.15.1.en: v If Jeremiah saw that those who were wounded in war deserved continual lamentation, what shall we say all the more for those calamities that befall souls?! (Isaiah) said: "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle" (Isa 22:2). I lament the sting of true death, and the gravity of sin, and the fiery darts of the evil one, those which kindle fires fiercely for souls as well as bodies.

22.15.2.en: Truly the divine commandment groans with a loud voice when it sees such uncleanness creeping over the earth, proclaiming in the Old Testament: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife" (Ex 20:17; Deut 5:21). And in the holy Gospel it also says: "Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:28). And here it now sees the very Bride of the Lord, she whose head is the Lord Christ, boldly committing the sin of adultery.

22.15.3.en: Even the congregations of the saints groan over her![11]

22.15.4.en: St. Basil the Great v Count every person better than yourself (Phil 2:3). Weep over your dead (see Sir 22:11; Jn 11:31). First cast the beam out of your own eye (Mt 7:5). Rebuild your house that was destroyed. Let him cry out: Have mercy on me, Son of David, that I may see again (Mk 10:47-51; Lk 18:38-41). Learn, you, until every mouth is stopped (Rom 3:19), and do not speak with arrogance. Make a bolt for your door (your mouth) [12].

22.15.5.en: Sts. Barsanuphius and John Do not prolong the discussion with the fool, and do not visit the dull; be on guard against him to avoid weariness, and do not be defiled by him if you come into contact with him.

22.16.0.en: Turn away from him and you will find rest, and you will not be wearied by his folly [13].

22.16.1.en: Ben Sira calls us not to enter into a discussion with a fool, lest we be defiled and be struck with a state of disturbance.

22.16.2.en: v When you meet a man who loves to argue, and he begins to dispute with you about what is self-evident and true, break off the conversation and withdraw quickly, for his mind has turned to stone. For just as water spoils the finest wines, so foolish arguments spoil those who are virtuous in conduct and in character [13].

22.16.3.en: St. Anthony the Great What is heavier than lead?

22.17.0.en: And what is his name but the fool? [14].

22.18.0.en: Sand and salt and a piece of iron are easier to carry than a foolish man [15].

22.19.0.en: The wooden brace bound into a building is not loosened by an earthquake; so also the firm mind fortified with rational counsel is not afraid of a crisis [16].

22.20.0.en: A mind established on wise thinking is like a plaster decoration on a polished wall [17].

22.20.1.en: Ben Sira compares the steadiness of the wise man with the unsteadiness of the fool. This steadiness or unsteadiness touches the life of the person in the midst of the community.

22.21.0.en: As fences set in a high place do not stand before the wind, so the cowardly heart in the thought of the fool does not stand before any kind of fear [18].

22.22.0.en: 24 He who pricks the eye brings forth tears, and he who pricks the heart brings out feeling. 25 He who throws a stone at birds frightens them away, and he who reproaches his friend breaks off the friendship. 26 If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for he will return. 27 If you open your mouth against your friend, do not be afraid, for he will be reconciled, except in reproach and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and a wound dealt with treachery; for in these every friend flees. 28 Remain faithful to your neighbor in his poverty, that you may be satisfied with him in his good things. 29 Stand by him in the time of his distress, that you may share in his inheritance. 30 Before the fire come the vapor of the furnace and the smoke; so before bloodshed come insults. 31 I am not ashamed to defend my friend, nor will I hide from his face; and even if evil befalls me from him, 32 everyone who hears of it will be on guard against him. 33 Who will set a guard over my mouth, and a sure seal upon my lips, that I may not fall because of them and my tongue destroy me?

22.22.1.en: The subject of friendship was very close to the heart of Ben Sira. For he longs to see society, if not the whole world, ruled by unity, love, tenderness and completeness. For wisdom in his mind does not stop at a person's ordering his own private life or enjoying eternal salvation, but touches the life of the community, if not of humanity as a whole!

22.22.2.en: The first part of this chapter speaks of wisdom, whose dangerous enemy is laziness; for the goal of wisdom and diligence, or constant perseverance, is that all humanity interact together in a spirit of genuine friendship. The fickle fool's evil returns upon the life of the community. Such a person cannot be relied upon. He is unsteady in his loyalty and faithfulness to others, therefore those who wish to form a friendship with him are struck with a state of frustration. There is no one who would like to keep the friendship of a person who is wrathful or abusive [20].

22.22.3.en: This does not mean that there is no anger between two faithful friends, but in the spirit of faithfulness the anger soon passes, and there may result from it a better love, trust and understanding.

22.22.4.en: He who pricks his eye makes tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out his feelings [19].

22.22.5.en: The scholar Origen[14] calls us to strike the eye and the heart with prayer in faith; we ask for God's work in us, and we ask for more of His gifts. As it came in the Psalms: "Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it" (Ps 81:11).

22.22.6.en: The phrase came in his writings: "He who pricks his eye, tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out feelings"; by the eye and the heart here he means the inner life. It befits the believer to drink from his inner springs, that is, from his insight and his affections. If the Word of God in His Incarnation dwelt among us, to establish His kingdom within us (Lk 17:21), then He directed our gaze to our depths, that we might see Him working in us. He came not despising us, but honoring us by our union with Him and our enjoyment of His surpassing works.

22.22.7.en: In the scholar Origen's discourse on the work of the Holy Spirit in man, he asks us to drink the living waters from our inner springs and wells, as it came in the Book of Proverbs (5:15, 18). It befits us to dig in our inner earth, that we may enjoy these living waters.

22.22.8.en: v Let us work according to the counsel of Wisdom to us, which says: "Drink waters out of your cistern, and running waters out of your well. Let them be yours..." (Prov 5:15, 17). Be assured, O reader, that you have your well and your spring, so that when you take hold of the Holy Bible, you begin to express yourself through your teaching of the text, in harmony with what you have learned from the Church, and also try to drink from your inner spiritual source.

22.22.9.en: Within you is a spring of living water (Gen 26:19), perennial veins, and an abundant flowing stream, with rational understanding so long as it does not collide with the earth and the remnants of rocks. Continue working to dig your earth and cleanse it of defilement, that you may remove laziness from yourself and drive idleness from your heart. Hear what the Holy Bible says: "Strike the eye and tears flow, and strike the heart and it produces understanding" [19]. You must also purify your spirit, so that you drink from your living springs. In truth, if you receive the Word of God within you, there becomes in you a spring of water overflowing with eternal life [15].

22.22.10.en: v You have the nature of living waters within you (Gen 26:19). There are in you perennial veins and channels overflowing with prudent understanding, provided only that they are not filled with dust and refuse.

22.22.11.en: Take care to dig your earth and remove the filth, that is, remove the idleness of your natural power, and drive out the idleness of your hearts. Hear what the Scripture says: "He who pricks the eye makes tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out understanding" (see Sir 22:19) [16].

22.22.12.en: v Continue to dig your earth and cleanse it of filth, that is, remove from it the idleness of your natural power, and drive out from it the idleness of your heart. The Scripture says: Strike the eye and tears flow, and strike the heart and understanding comes forth [17].

22.22.13.en: The scholar Origen v Preserve, my children, that friendship which you began with your brothers, for there is nothing in the world more beautiful than this. It is a comfort in this life to have one to whom you can open your heart, share your trust, and entrust with the secrets of your heart. It is a comfort to have beside you a trustworthy person who rejoices with you in your prosperity, sympathizes with you in your troubles, and encourages you in persecution.

22.22.14.en: What good friends were those Hebrew youths whom the flame of the furnace's fires did not separate from their love for one another (Dan 3:16 etc.)! We say of them what was said: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided" (2 Sam 1:23) [18].

22.22.15.en: v He who is not faithful to God cannot be a friend to a person. Friendship is the guardian of godliness and the teacher of equality, making the greater equal to the lesser, and the lesser to the greater [19].

22.22.16.en: v Friendship cannot exist where there is false flattery [20].

22.22.17.en: St. Ambrose Throwing a stone at birds makes them flee in fright, and insulting a friend breaks off the friendship [20].

22.22.18.en: Sirach warns us lest we lose friendship through some trivial behavior that we practice. For friends leave a person quickly when they sense a danger coming upon them, like birds that flee if someone throws a stone toward them.

22.22.19.en: It befits a person to hasten to apologize for his wrong conduct without justifying himself; if he has uttered a harsh word or drawn a sword against his friend, let him not despair of regaining the friendship if he is earnest about it.

22.22.20.en: He who draws near to his neighbor in the time of his distress, the friend most often forgets this when he comes into prosperity.

22.22.21.en: It befits a person not to be ashamed to defend his friend in the time of his poverty or distress, and not to try to flee from him.

22.22.22.en: If evil befalls you from your friend, take care not to sin with a word against him.

22.22.23.en: If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for renewing the friendship is possible [21].

22.22.24.en: v Let us follow love, for it is a safety valve that does not allow us to suffer any evil. Let us bind ourselves to one another. Would that there be no deceit among us and no lie. For where friendship exists there is nothing of the kind. The wise man also tells us: "If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for the friendship can be renewed. If you open your mouth against your friend, do not be afraid, for reconciliation may take place, except in the case of abuse and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and the treacherous blow. For in these cases every friend flees"... What secret do you have? Do you wish to do evil to your brother? Or do you wish to deprive him of sharing with you some benefits? For this reason the secret must be annulled! [21]

22.22.25.en: St. John Chrysostom If you open your mouth against a friend, do not be afraid, for reconciliation is possible, except in abuse and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and the blow of treachery; for every friend flees from conduct like this [22].

22.22.26.en: When someone discloses the secret of his friend, what concerns the friend is not his material or moral losses because of the disclosure of the secret, but rather the loss of trust and the lack of faithfulness.

22.22.27.en: v Nothing is good without friendship... Let one person have a hill of talents, and another have a hundred friends; the latter is richer in his resources than the former.

22.22.28.en: St. John Chrysostom Gain the trust of your neighbor in his poverty, and you may be satisfied with him in his prosperity.

22.22.29.en: Stand with him in the time of distress, and you may share with him in his inheritance [23].

22.23.0.en: The true, faithful friend is known by his steadfastness in practical friendship and his concern if the friend is struck by poverty or want or distress. True friendship is manifested when the friend does all in his power to protect him from his enemy [25].

22.23.1.en: Just as the smoke and vapor of the furnace precede the fire, so insult precedes bloodshed [24].

22.23.2.en: I am not ashamed to protect a friend, nor will I hide from his face [25].

22.24.0.en: And if evil befalls me because of him, everyone who hears of it will be on guard against him [26].

22.24.1.en: v If friendship proceeds from the fountain of good will, do not hesitate to endure great dangers in life for the sake of the friend. It is said: If evils befall me from him, I will bear them [22].

22.24.2.en: v Surely, if there is a necessity to give testimony, whoever knows a fault in a friend of his must rebuke him privately, and if he does not listen he must do so openly. For rebuke is good, and is often better than silent friendship. Even if the friend thinks that he has been hurt, you must rebuke him. And if the bitterness of the wounds to his mind is for his correction, do not cease from rebuking him; do not be afraid!

22.24.3.en: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Prov 27:6). So rebuke your erring friend, and do not abandon the innocent. For friendship must be faithful and settled in true affection. It befits us not to exchange our friends in a childish way for a trivial passion [23].

22.24.4.en: v In necessity we endure even troubles for the sake of the friend. Even enmity can be endured for the innocence of the friend. We endure even insults if someone defends and answers for a friend who wrongs him and charges him with (false) accusations. Do not be afraid of such troubles, for the voice of the righteous man says: "And if evil befall me from him, I will bear it for the sake of the friend" (see Sir 22:6).

22.24.5.en: In the time of hardship also the friend appears, for in the time of ease all seem to be friends. And just as patience and endurance are required in the time of trial, so in the time of ease the strong influence (of friends) is required to examine and refute the arrogance of the domineering friend [24].

22.24.6.en: St. Ambrose Who will set a guard over my mouth, and the seal of prudence upon my lips, that I may not fall because of them, and my tongue not destroy me?

22.24.7.en: v It does not befit a person to open his mouth for what is unseemly, but to open it for speech that bestows treasures of God's goods.

22.24.8.en: Fr. Anthimus of Jerusalem v Let us keep in mind, concerning the mouth and the tongue, that we offer our prayer while keeping them free from evil. If you have a vessel of gold or made of precious metal, you do not choose it to use for a shameful matter; how much more those whose mouths are more precious than gold and pearls, how can they defile them with shameful ugliness and corruption and mockery. You do not offer incense on an altar of bronze or even of gold, but what is more precious than this in a spiritual temple, for the material of the former is lifeless, while God makes His dwelling in you, you who are members of the body of Christ... Let us guard our mouths always; let us set a mind over them to close them, so that they are not kept closed continually, but it opens them at the proper time.

22.24.9.en: There is a time when silence is more precious than speech, and there is also a time when speech is more precious than silence... It is necessary, as you see, not only that we keep silence and speech at the proper time, but that it be with great love. For this reason Paul also says: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man" (Col 4:6).

22.24.10.en: Bear in mind that this is the member with which you enter into converse with God, and with which we offer the praise. This is the member with which we receive the awesome Sacrifice, for the faithful know what I am saying [25].

22.24.11.en: St. John Chrysostom Inspired by Sirach 22

22.25.s.en: O Holy One, sanctify my children and my friends!

22.25.0.en: v Your descent to our earth has turned my heart into a sanctuary for You, from which You establish a temple in which Your Holy Spirit dwells.

22.25.1.en: You removed the dust from it, and springs of living water burst forth within me!

22.25.2.en: My heart has been kindled with the fire of Your love, so I see in the young my children, and in the old friends and beloved ones.

22.25.3.en: How my depths long that the whole new generation (the children) be sanctified, and with it the present generation (the friends).

22.25.4.en: v I confess to You my laziness and slackness, for I caused my children to stumble.

22.25.5.en: Remove the stumbling block from them, and instead of laziness let them work by You, O Almighty.

22.25.6.en: For their sake You did not cease working for their salvation.

22.25.7.en: You loved them and were crucified for them, and here You are preparing for them glorious mansions in Your heavens.

22.25.8.en: Fill them with the spirit of wisdom, that they may walk in purity and chastity and love and longsuffering.

22.25.9.en: They will become a living icon of You, so that the heavenly ones marvel at Your work in them.

22.25.10.en: v Shine the light of Your knowledge in their hearts, that they may reject folly and ignorance.

22.25.11.en: They will accept from You rebuke and discipline for their edification on a heavenly level.

22.25.12.en: Glory to You, who stretched out Your hands on the Cross; here You embrace all generations.

22.25.13.en: v And what shall I say of my brothers? They are my friends and my beloved.

22.25.14.en: Burst forth in their hearts springs of spiritual water, that will turn their dust into holy, fruitful spiritual gardens.

22.25.15.en: v Sanctify my tongue and theirs, that they may become instruments of righteousness bearing witness to Your salvation.

22.25.16.en: Instead of idle chatter and harsh words and the disclosing of others' secrets, grant me and them the holy tongue, the sweet words, and the constant smile.

22.25.17.en: We will not entrust the guard of our tongues, able to tame our mouths, to any but Your Holy Spirit.

22.25.18.en: How easy it is to tame wild beasts and teach birds, but the taming of our tongues is Your work alone!

22.25.19.en: v Grant us the spirit of trustworthiness and faithfulness, so that in the distress of our friends we find an opportunity to serve them with joy, to express by it our pure and sincere love for them.
